tasks.title: A motor command from the log in percent of travel
tasks.statement: DShot, the log header `motorOutput:{lo},2047`. The median of `motor[1]` over the hover segment is **{m}**. Find the motor output in percent of travel.
tasks.solution: p = (motor − low)/(high − low)·100. The lower limit 158 = 48 + 0.055·1999 with `dshot_idle_value` 550; 48 — when dynamic idle is enabled (`dyn_idle_min_rpm` > 0). The upper limit is 2047 with `motor_output_limit` 100.

tasks.title: The rear–front imbalance index
tasks.statement: The motor medians over a level segment, % of travel: 1 RR **{a}**, 2 FR **{b}**, 3 RL **{c}**, 4 FL **{d}**. Find I_pitch (rear minus front) in percent of the mean.
tasks.solution: I_pitch = [(p₁ + p₃) − (p₂ + p₄)]/2/p̄·100: the difference of the averages of the rear and front pairs, divided by the mean of all four. Positive — the rear ones work harder (the CG is to the rear, or a front corner is “stronger”); a cause is never assigned from a single index.

tasks.title: An estimate of the center-of-gravity offset
tasks.statement: I_pitch = **{i} %** (in terms of the command, I_roll and I_yaw are near zero). The distance between the front and rear motor axes is **{L} mm**. The index in terms of thrust is **k = {k}** times the index in terms of the command (thrust ∝ command^k, k measured on a thrust stand). Estimate the rearward CG offset, mm.
tasks.solution: The balance of moments: T_front·(L/2 + x) = T_rear·(L/2 − x) → x = I_T·L/4, where I_T is the index in terms of thrust (as a fraction). I_T = k·I_pitch, so x = k·I_pitch·L/4. Per the 15×5 table from `des-thrust-stand`, k ≈ 1.1–1.8; k = 2 is the upper bound, if the RPM is taken as proportional to the command.

tasks.title: How weak motor 4 is with an offset CG
tasks.statement: The medians, % of travel: 1 RR **{a}**, 2 FR **{b}**, 3 RL **{c}**, 4 FL **{d}**. The swap test showed that the defect is motor 4, and there are no causes other than an offset CG. By how many percent more command does motor 4 need?
tasks.solution: With an offset CG alone the motors obey p₁ + p₄ = p₂ + p₃, so motor 4 “should” have p₂ + p₃ − p₁ (the neighbors minus the opposite one). w = p₄/(p₂ + p₃ − p₁) − 1.
